sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.2.4 (Uniform convergence theorem for regularly varying functions) … lim_{x→∞} f(tx)/f(x) = t^α, uniformly in t (a) on each [a, b] if α = 0, (b) on each (0, b] if α > 0, (c) on each [a, ∞) if α < 0.
sources.attribution: © T. Mikosch. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: The excerpt omits the source hypothesis that f is regularly varying with index α, and bounded on each interval (0, x] when α > 0. Each of the three source cases contains uniformity on every compact interval [c, d] ⊂ (0, ∞), which is the authored statement for every index, with no boundedness condition. The source states the theorem without proof. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 1.3 (uniform convergence theorem) in Geluk and de Haan, CWI Tract 40 (1987), pp. 4-5.

sources.module: Chapter 1, Section 1.2 Basic Properties
sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.2.1 (Representation theorem) A positive measurable function L on [x₀, ∞) is slowly varying if and only if it can be written in the form L(x) = c(x) exp{∫_{x₀}^x ε(y)/y dy} (1.2) where c(·) is a measurable non-negative function such that lim_{x→∞} c(x) = c₀ ∈ (0, ∞) and ε(x) → 0 as x → ∞.
sources.attribution: © T. Mikosch. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: The source states the theorem for slowly varying L, with the lower limit x₀ of the integral at the left end of the domain. The authored statement also requires ε to be measurable and bounded on bounded intervals, so that the integral exists, and adds the form for regularly varying functions that the source gives in Remark 1.2.2. The source gives no proof. The authored proof follows the proof of Theorem 1.5 (representation theorem) in Geluk and de Haan, CWI Tract 40 (1987), p. 8, which uses formula (1.14) from the proof of Karamata's theorem on p. 7.

sources.module: Chapter I, Section I.1 Regularly varying functions
sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.2 Suppose f: ℝ⁺ → ℝ is measurable, eventually positive and … (1.6) exists, is finite and positive for all x in a set of positive Lebesgue measure, then f ∈ RV_α for some α ∈ ℝ.
sources.attribution: © J. L. Geluk and L. de Haan. Quoted from CWI Tract 40 for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: In the source, (1.6) is the limit lim_{t→∞} f(tx)/f(t), and f is defined on (0, ∞) and eventually positive. The authored statement takes f positive on [a, ∞) and asks the set of x to be measurable. The authored proof follows the source proof on pp. 3-4: it passes to F(t) = log f(e^t), uses Steinhaus' theorem to show that the limit exists for every x, and solves the additive equation (1.7). For the last step it uses Steinhaus' theorem a second time instead of Lusin's theorem.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.4 (Karamata's theorem) Suppose f ∈ RV_α. There exists t₀ > 0 such that f(t) is positive and locally bounded for t ≥ t₀. If α ≥ −1, then lim_{t→∞} t f(t)/∫_{t₀}^t f(s) ds = α + 1. If α < −1, or α = −1 and ∫_0^∞ f(s) ds < ∞, then lim_{t→∞} t f(t)/∫_t^∞ f(s) ds = −α − 1. Conversely: if (1.8) holds with −1 < α < ∞, then f ∈ RV_α; if (1.9) holds with −∞ < α < −1, then f ∈ RV_α.
sources.attribution: © J. L. Geluk and L. de Haan. Quoted from CWI Tract 40 for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: The source states the theorem for f ∈ RV_α with integrals from a point t₀ beyond which f is positive and locally bounded, and it gives the converse for −1 < α < ∞ and for α < −1. The authored statement writes the case α = −1 separately and writes the converse with the limit c = α + 1 or c = −α − 1. The authored proof follows the source proof on pp. 5-7: dyadic blocks, regular variation of the integral, the limit (1.11) from the uniform convergence theorem, and the converse through b(t) = t f(t)/F(t). For the converse it integrates (log F)' = b(t)/t directly instead of using formula (1.14).

sources.excerpt: (Karamata's Tauberian theorem) Let U be a non-decreasing, right-continuous function defined on [0, ∞). If L is slowly varying, c ≥ 0, α ≥ 0, then the following are equivalent: (a) U(x) ∼ c x^α L(x)/Γ(1 + α), x → ∞, (b) Û(s) = ∫_0^∞ e^{−sx} dU(x) ∼ c s^{−α} L(1/s), s ↓ 0. When c = 0, (a) is to be interpreted as U(x) = o(x^α L(x)) as x → ∞, similarly for (b).
sources.attribution: © T. Mikosch. Quoted from the author's lecture notes for identification of the cited result.

sources.alignment: The authored statement is Theorem 1.2.10 of the source with the convention U(x) = 0 for x < 0 written out, so that dU includes the jump U(0) at 0. It also states that Û is finite in (b), and it adds the relation U(x) ∼ Û(1/x)/Γ(1 + α) for c > 0, which the source gives as (c) after the theorem. The source states the theorem without proof and refers to Bingham, Goldie and Teugels. The authored proof uses Karamata's polynomial method for the Tauberian direction.

sources.excerpt: Lemma 2.2.1 (Basic properties of subexponential distributions) (a) If F ∈ S, then uniformly on compact y-sets of (0, ∞), lim_{x→∞} F̄(x − y)/F̄(x) = 1. (2.2) (b) If (2.2) holds then, for all ε > 0, e^{εx} F̄(x) → ∞, x → ∞. (c) If F ∈ S then, given ε > 0, there exists a finite constant K so that for all n ≥ 2, F̄^{n∗}(x)/F̄(x) ≤ K(1 + ε)^n, x ≥ 0. (2.3)

sources.alignment: Parts (a), (b) and (d) of the authored statement are parts (a), (b) and (c) of the source. The source defines F ∈ S by F̄^{n∗}(x) ∼ n F̄(x) for all n ≥ 2 (Definition 2.1.1). The authored statement assumes this only for n = 2 and proves the case of general n as part (c), which the source attributes to Chistyakov in Remark 2.1.2 on p. 35. sources.excerpt: (Properties of the Hill estimator) Suppose (Xn) is strictly stationary with marginal distribution F satisfying for some α > 0 and slowly varying L, F̄(x) = P(X > x) = x^{−α}L(x), x > 0. Let α̂^{(H)} = α̂^{(H)}_{k,n} be the Hill estimator (1.31). (a) (Weak consistency) Assume that one of the following conditions is satisfied: (Xn) is iid, (Xn) is weakly dependent, (Xn) is a linear process. If k → ∞, k/n → 0 for n → ∞, then α̂^{(H)} →P α.

sources.alignment: The authored statement is the iid case of part (a) of Theorem 1.4.44. The source estimator (1.31) uses the k-th largest value X_{k,n} as the threshold. The authored statement uses X_{k+1,n} and covers the source form as a variant. It also says what happens on the event X_{k+1,n} ≤ 0. The source gives no proof. sources.module: Section 2.1 The Extremal Types Theorem for stationary sequences
sources.excerpt: Theorem 2.1.2. (Extremal Types Theorem for Stationary Sequences) Let {ξ_n} be a stationary sequence such that M_n = max(ξ_1, ξ_2, …, ξ_n) has a non-degenerate limiting distribution G as in (1.2.1). Suppose that D(u_n) holds for each u_n of the form u_n = x/a_n + b_n, for x with 0 < G(x) < 1. Then G is one of the three classical extremal types.
sources.attribution: © M. R. Leadbetter and Holger Rootzén. Quoted from the University of Copenhagen preprint for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: The source asks for D(u_n) only at the levels with 0 < G(x) < 1. The authored statement asks for D(u_n) at every real x, which is a stronger hypothesis. With it, step s3 gives convergence at every continuity point of G without an extra argument at the levels where G(x) = 0. The outline follows the proof that the source indicates: Lemma 2.1.1, max-stability of G as in [66, Theorem 3.3.3], and the classification of max-stable laws.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 2.2.1 Let the stationary sequence {ξ_n} have extremal index θ > 0. If P{a_n(M̂_n − b_n) ≤ x} → G(x) then P{a_n(M_n − b_n) ≤ x} → G^θ(x) and conversely. That is M_n has an asymptotic distribution if and only if M̂_n does, with the power relation between the limits and the same normalizing constants.

The source says that the level form follows by obvious arguments from [64] (Leadbetter, 1983). The steps write out these arguments and then take v_n = x/a_n + b_n, as the source does.

sources.module: Chapter 7 The Reserve Process and the Ruin Problem, Section 7.3 Lundberg’s Inequality, result 7.3.4
sources.excerpt: Theorem (Lundberg’s Inequality). If ρ ∈ (0, ∞) is a superadjustment coefficient for the excess premium process, then the identity P[{inf_{n∈N₀} U_n^u < 0}] ≤ e^{−ρu} holds for all u ∈ (0, ∞).
sources.attribution: © Klaus D. Schmidt. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Lectures on Risk Theory for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: The source numbers the result 7.3.4 and states it for the modified reserve process U_n^u = u + Σ (κW_k − X_k), with independent excess premiums and a superadjustment coefficient ρ. Its Lemma 7.1.2 shows that ruin of the continuous-time reserve happens only at claim times. The authored statement restricts to i.i.d. excess premiums and states the ruin event in continuous time. The authored proof follows the source: a nonnegative supermartingale e^(−ρU_n) and a maximal bound, here obtained by optional stopping.

sources.module: Chapter 1 Introduction, Section 1.2 The Classical Problem of Ruin
sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.3 (Pollaczek–Khintchine formula) Suppose that λμ/c < 1. For all x ≥ 0, 1 − P_x(τ_0^− < ∞) = (1 − ρ) Σ_{k≥0} ρ^k η^{*k}(x), where ρ = λμ/c, η(x) = (1/μ) ∫_0^x (1 − F(y)) dy, x ≥ 0, and, for k ≥ 0, we understand η^{*k} to be the k-fold convolution of η with the special understanding that η^{*0}(dx) = δ_0(dx).

sources.alignment: The source writes the integrated tail distribution as η and the ruin probability as P_x(τ_0^− < ∞), with τ_0^− = inf{t > 0 : X_t < 0}. The authored statement adds the equivalent form for ψ and the value ψ(0) = ρ. The source proves the formula later with scale functions. The authored proof follows instead the classical renewal argument of first-claim conditioning, as in Bingham's lecture notes, and solves the renewal equation by iteration.

sources.module: Section 2 Veraverbeke’s Theorem
sources.excerpt: Theorem 1 (Veraverbeke). (i) Suppose that, in addition to (4), F^s is long-tailed. Then lim inf_{x→∞} P(M > x)/F̄^s(x) ≥ 1/a. (ii) Suppose that, in addition to (4), F^s is subexponential. Then lim_{x→∞} P(M > x)/F̄^s(x) = 1/a.
sources.attribution: © Stan Zachary. Quoted from the author's arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: The source states the result for the maximum M of a random walk with i.i.d. increments of mean −a < 0 and second tail F^s. In the Cramér–Lundberg model ψ(u) = P(M > u) for the increments ξ_k − cW_k, with a = c/λ − μ, and the second tail of these increments is asymptotic to μ(1 − F_I(u)) because F_I is long-tailed. So part (ii) gives the same limit ρ/(1 − ρ). The authored proof does not follow the one-big-jump proof of the source: it follows the Pollaczek–Khinchine and dominated convergence route of Embrechts and Veraverbeke, as presented in Mikosch's survey, relations (2.8)-(2.11).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 4.6.1 (The elementary renewal theorem). Let {N(t); t > 0} be a renewal counting process with mean inter-renewal interval X̄. Then lim_{t→∞} E[N(t)]/t = 1/X̄.

sources.module: Section 2, The Feller-Erdös-Pollard renewal theorem
sources.excerpt: Theorem 1. (Feller-Erdös-Pollard) Let (Sn)n≥0 be an ordinary arithmetic renewal process whose inter-occurrence time distribution fk = P{Xi = k} has finite mean 0 < µ < ∞ and is not supported by any proper additive subgroup of the integers (i.e., there is no m ≥ 2 such that P{Xi ∈ mZ} = 1). Let u be the associated renewal measure. Then lim_{k→∞} u(k) = lim_{k→∞} P{Sn = k for some n ≥ 0} = 1/µ.
sources.attribution: © Steven P. Lalley. Quoted from the author's lecture notes Renewal Theory for identification of the cited result.

sources.alignment: The source states the theorem for a finite mean and proves it with a Markov chain and with a coupling. The authored statement works with the renewal equation (the source's Proposition 1) and includes the infinite mean case with limit 0, as in the original paper of Erdős, Feller and Pollard (Bull. Amer. Math. Soc. 55 (1949), 201-204). The authored proof follows the elementary proof of that paper on pp. 203-204, with an explicit Bézout bound for the representation of large integers.

sources.module: Chapter 7, Section 7.5.1 Wald's identity for two thresholds
sources.excerpt: Theorem 7.5.1 (Wald's identity). Let {Xi; i ≥ 1} be IID and let γ(r) = ln{E[e^{rX}]} be the semi-invariant MGF of each Xi. Assume γ(r) is finite in the open interval (r−, r+) with r− < 0 < r+. For each n ≥ 1, let Sn = X1 + · · · + Xn. Let α > 0 and β < 0 be arbitrary real numbers, and let J be the smallest n for which either Sn ≥ α or Sn ≤ β. Then for all r ∈ (r−, r+), E[exp(rSJ − Jγ(r))] = 1.
sources.attribution: © Robert G. Gallager. Quoted from the MIT OpenCourseWare notes Discrete Stochastic Processes, Chapter 7, for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: The source assumes that γ is finite on an open interval around 0 and takes r in that interval. Its proof treats discrete steps and uses Lemma 7.5.1 (p. 335) for the finiteness of J, which needs steps that are not identically 0. The authored statement makes this condition explicit, includes the geometric tail bound of Lemma 7.5.1, and allows every r with E e^(rX₁) < ∞. The authored proof follows the tilting proof of the source for a general step law with product measures.

There the scale function is W^(q)(x) = (e^{(δ−ω)x} − e^{−(δ+ω)x})/(σ²δ) with δ = σ^{−2}(µ² + 2qσ²)^{1/2} and ω = µ/σ². So θ+ = δ − ω, θ− = −(δ + ω), and the source's c* equals the authored c*. sources.excerpt: 1) Classical Secretary Problem. … An observation at time k is a record if and only if his relative rank among the first k variables is 1. It is known that pk = 1/k. … The s index in the odds theorem can be computed and gives the optimal strategy. It is the largest s such that ∑_{j=s}^n (j − 1)^{−1} ≥ 1. Therefore V(n) = ((s − 1)/n) ∑_{j=s−1}^{n−1} j^{−1}. Note that s = s(n) ∼ n/e and thus V(n) → 1/e.

sources.alignment: The source derives the secretary rule as the first application of its Theorem 1, the odds theorem of Bruss, in the paragraph that follows the theorem. It gives the threshold s and the value V(n), and states s(n) ∼ n/e and V(n) → 1/e without proof. The authored statement makes the model explicit, and the authored proof adds the independence of the relative ranks, the reduction to the odds theorem and the integral bounds for the limits.

sources.module: Section 1, Introduction and main results
sources.excerpt: Theorem 1 ([3], Bruss’ odds theorem of optimal stopping) An optimal stopping rule τ ∈ L is to stop at the first index k ≥ s (if such exists) with Ik = 1, where s = max{1, max{l : ∑_{j=l}^n rj ≥ 1}}, with the convention max{∅} = −∞. The corresponding probability of “winning” is Vn := P(Iτ = 1, Iτ+1 = 0, . . . , In = 0) = ∏_{j=s}^n qj ∑_{l=s}^n rl.

sources.alignment: The source restates Bruss's theorem (its reference [3]) with the filtration generated by I_1, …, I_k. sources.excerpt: Theorem 7.33 (Tanaka's formula) Let {B(t) : t ⩾ 0} be linear Brownian motion. Then, for every a ∈ R, almost surely, for all t > 0, |B(t) − a| − |B(0) − a| = ∫_0^t sign(B(s) − a) dB(s) + L^a(t), where sign x = 1{x>0} − 1{x<0}.

sources.alignment: Theorem 7.33 (Tanaka's formula) on p. 210 states that for linear Brownian motion and every a ∈ R, almost surely, for all t > 0, |B(t) − a| − |B(0) − a| = ∫₀ᵗ sign(B(s) − a) dB(s) + L^a(t), where L^a(t) is the continuous occupation density of Theorem 6.19. The authored statement defines L^a as the L² limit of (1/(2ε))∫1{|B − a| < ε} ds and adds the monotonicity and support properties. Where the occupation measure has a continuous density, (1/(2ε)) times the occupation measure of (a − ε, a + ε) converges to that density, so the two local times agree. The source proves the formula with Lemma 7.36 (a smooth convolution and Itô's formula) and the occupation density. The authored proof instead applies Itô's formula to a C¹ function that is quadratic on (a − ε, a + ε) and equal to |y − a| outside.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 2.1. Consider the stochastic differential equation (1.2). Assume that there exist a constant γ > 0 and functions κ, ϱ: [0, γ] → [0, ∞) satisfying κ(0) = 0, |b(t, x) − b(t, y)| ≤ κ(|x − y|), and ‖σ(t, x) − σ(t, y)‖_F ≤ ϱ(|x − y|) for all t ∈ [0, ∞) and x, y ∈ ℝⁿ with |x − y| ≤ γ. Furthermore, assume that ϱ is non-decreasing, ϱ(u) > 0 for all u ∈ (0, γ] and its square satisfies the Osgood condition … Then the pathwise uniqueness of solutions of (1.2) holds for every initial distribution µ.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.1 (Freedman). Consider a real-valued martingale {Y_k : k = 0, 1, 2, …} with difference sequence {X_k : k = 1, 2, 3, …}. Assume that the difference sequence is uniformly bounded: X_k ≤ R almost surely for k = 1, 2, 3, …. Define the predictable quadratic variation process of the martingale: W_k := ∑_{j=1}^k E_{j−1} X_j² for k = 1, 2, 3, …. Then, for all t ≥ 0 and σ² > 0, P{∃k ≥ 0 : Y_k ≥ t and W_k ≤ σ²} ≤ exp(−(t²/2)/(σ² + Rt/3)).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1. Let X be a one-dimensional random variable with mean µ, and P(X ∈ (a, b)) = 1, where −∞ ≤ a < b ≤ ∞. Let ϕ(x) is a twice differentiable function on (a, b), and define function h(x; ν) ≜ (ϕ(x) − ϕ(ν))/(x − ν)² − ϕ′(ν)/(x − ν). Then inf_{x∈(a,b)} {h(x; µ)} var(X) ≤ E[ϕ(X)] − ϕ(E[X]) ≤ sup_{x∈(a,b)} {h(x; µ)} var(X).
sources.attribution: © J. G. Liao and Arthur Berg. Quoted from the arXiv preprint for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: The source takes the infimum and the supremum of h over (a, b) and leaves the point x = μ and the integrability of φ(X) implicit. The authored statement excludes x = μ, assumes E[X²] < ∞, and states each bound separately with the exact condition under which E[φ(X)] exists. Part (iii) is the remark that follows Theorem 1 in the source. The authored proof follows the source proof, which integrates the exact second-order expansion φ(x) = φ(μ) + φ′(μ)(x − μ) + h(x)(x − μ)² against the law of X.

Fix x, y ∈ X, and let (x₀, x₁, …, x_r) be a path achieving the minimum in (14.5). By the triangle inequality for ρ_K, ρ_K(P(x, ·), P(y, ·)) ≤ ∑_{k=1}^r ρ_K(P(x_{k−1}, ·), P(x_k, ·)).

sources.excerpt: Theorem 5.2 (Lieb’s theorem) Consider a bipartite Hubbard model. We assume |Λ| is even, and the whole Λ is connected through nonvanishing tx,y. We also assume Ux = U > 0 for any x ∈ Λ. Then the ground states of the model are nondegenerate apart from the trivial spin degeneracy, and have total spin Stot = ||A| − |B||/2.
sources.attribution: © Hal Tasaki. Quoted from the author's arXiv version of the review for identification of the cited result.
sources.reuse: Short quotation for citation only. The statement, proof and application of this record are authored for this catalog.
sources.alignment: The source states Lieb's theorem for the half-filled Hubbard model in the form of the authored statement. Its Definition 5.1 on pp. 15-16 defines bipartite as t_xy = 0 whenever x and y lie in the same sublattice. Section 5 of the source concerns half filling, N = |Λ|, and the source gives no proof. The outline follows the presentation of Lieb's 1989 proof by Freericks, which uses the partial particle-hole transformation, spin-reflection positivity, the U-continuity and the Lieb-Mattis theorem.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.1 (Ordering of Energy Levels [14]) Suppose the Heisenberg Hamiltonian HΛ,J is irreducible and (A, B)-bipartite. Define S̄ = |SA − SB|. Then E(Λ, S + 1) > E(Λ, S) for all S ≥ S̄, E(Λ, S) > E(Λ, S̄) for S < S̄.
sources.attribution: © Bruno Nachtergaele, Wolfgang Spitzer and Shannon Starr. Quoted from the authors' arXiv version of the paper for identification of the cited result.

sources.alignment: The source states the Lieb-Mattis theorem for irreducible (A, B)-bipartite Heisenberg models with arbitrary spins, as defined on its p. 2. The authored statement uses the same conditions, adds the uniqueness of the ground multiplet and the Marshall sign rule, and requires both sets to be nonempty. The authored proof follows the Perron-Frobenius sketch on pp. 3-4 of the source. It replaces the continuity argument of the sketch by the original comparison of positive ground vectors with the model S_A·S_B.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 1.1. Let S_N be the group of all permutations of N numbers with uniform distribution and let l_N(π) be the length of the longest increasing subsequence of π ∈ S_N. Let χ be a random variable whose distribution function is F. Then, as N → ∞, χ_N ≡ (l_N − 2√N)/N^(1/6) → χ in distribution.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 2.1. If (A) holds, then (1) holds. … Proposition 2.1. Let {X_pk} be independent random variables with EX_pk = 0, EX²_pk = 1 for each p ⩾ 1. Then (2) holds if and only if (A) holds for x_p = (X_p1, …, X_pp), p ⩾ 1.

sources.alignment: Yaskov's Theorem 2.1 proves the almost sure convergence (1) to the Marchenko–Pastur law for matrices with i.i.d. columns under his assumption (A) on quadratic forms. With Proposition 2.1 and the Lindeberg condition (2), which holds for i.i.d. entries with variance 1, it gives the authored statement. The authored proof follows his resolvent method, but proves the quadratic-form bound directly by truncation, writes out the martingale concentration step, and identifies the limit by Stieltjes inversion instead of a citation of Bai and Zhou.

sources.excerpt: Proposition 5.4. (Extinction Criterion) Provided p₁ ≠ 1, we have (i) q = 1 ⇔ f′(1) ≤ 1; (ii) q is the smallest root of f(s) = s in [0, 1] – the only other possible root being 1.

The authored statement uses the mean m, allows m = ∞, and adds that q < 1 is the only root in [0, 1) when m > 1. The authored proof follows the generating-function argument of Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorems 4.3.10 to 4.3.12, pp. 231-233, and replaces the martingale step for m ≤ 1 by the inequality 1 − f(s) ≤ m(1 − s).

sources.excerpt: Theorem A: Supercritical Processes (Kesten and Stigum (1966)). Suppose that 1 < m < ∞ and let W be the limit of the martingale Zn/mn. The following are equivalent: (i) P[W = 0] = q; (ii) E[W] = 1; (iii) E[L log+ L] < ∞.

The authored proof follows Sections 2 and 3 of the source: size-biased trees, the density W_n on the first n levels, and Seneta's dichotomy for immigration (Theorem 3.1). It proves the two parts of the measure-change dichotomy (3.2) and (3.3) that the source cites from Durrett, and it proves Proposition 3.2 with the extinction criterion.

sources.excerpt: Theorem 9.10 (Thomson's Principle). For any finite connected graph, R(a ↔ z) = inf{E(θ) : θ a unit flow from a to z}. The unique minimizer in the inf above is the unit current flow.
sources.attribution: © David A. Levin and Yuval Peres. Quoted from Markov Chains and Mixing Times, second edition, for identification of the cited result.

The authored statement includes the existence of the voltage and adds the exact energy identity E(θ) = R(a ↔ z) + E(θ − i). The source proves the theorem by compactness and the cycle law (Proposition 9.4). The authored proof uses the orthogonal decomposition of a flow into the current and a sourceless flow, as in Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks, Section 2.4, equation (2.10).

duplicate_exclusions.name: De Haan's spectral representation of max-stable processes
duplicate_exclusions.reason:
de-haan-max-stable-representation: no open source with a proof that I can outline.

Searches and downloads (about 9):
1. de Haan (1984), Ann. Probab. 12, 1194-1204, on Project Euclid: the download gives an HTML page, not the PDF.
2. Dombry, "A guided tour in the theory of max-stable processes", slides, Fields Institute, May 2016
   (https://homepages.uc.edu/~wangyz/misc/2016Workshop/Dombry.pdf): "Theorem (de Haan 1984, Gine et al. 1990)"
   on slide 17/74 states the representation, but the slides give no proof.
3. Oesting, Schlather and Zhou, arXiv 1310.1813: cites de Haan (1984) and de Haan and Ferreira (2006), Cor. 9.4.4.
   No proof of the existence of the representation.
4. Wang and Stoev, arXiv 0903.3594: Proposition 2.1 (p. 5) states the representation over [0,1] under Condition S.
   Its proof is one line: "follows from Proposition 3.2 in [35]" (Stoev and Taqqu, Extremes 8, 2005).
5. Stoev and Taqqu (2005), Extremes 8: no open copy found. Stoev's publication page returns 403.
6. Kabluchko, "Spectral representations of sum- and max-stable processes", Extremes 12 (2009), Theorem 1:
   Springer gives a bot-check page. There is no arXiv version (arXiv API search).
7. Oesting, arXiv 1707.02912, and Hashorva, arXiv 1605.03208: both use de Haan (1984) as a black box.
8. Davydov, Molchanov and Zuyev, arXiv math/0512196: Example 8.7 gives only the finite-dimensional
   (coordinatewise maximum) LePage representation, not the process result.
9. A general web search for lecture notes with a proof found none.

An outline must state the real steps of a published proof. Without an open copy of de Haan (1984),
Stoev and Taqqu (2005), Kabluchko (2009) or de Haan and Ferreira (2006), Chapter 9, I cannot do that.
